Earlier coverage experiment · Earlier learning report

Self-generated practice and the elicitation gap

Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct · fixed arithmetic questions · linear Gaussian mechanism · September 6, 2026

The same initial model answered 0.7% of fresh questions correctly with a short answer, 80.6% with one reasoning trace, and 88.2% with four-trace consensus. This confirms a gap in access to existing competence under the specified response procedures.

Answer-only consolidation failed. Across three optimization seeds, final-answer training produced almost no accuracy on new questions and sharply reduced reasoning under the reasoning prompt. Fresh self-produced targets then became mostly wrong. Retaining full self-generated traces in context did help: reasoning accuracy rose from 84.0% to 94.4% in an exploratory check.

A new full-trace training recipe tests whether reasoning survives when its actual computations are retained. From a common 84.0% reasoning baseline, final accuracy is 87.5% with a frozen source and 100.0% with a current source. This follow-up has one optimization seed; its full results and limits appear below.

The unchanged full-trace recipe was then repeated on new practice and evaluation questions with three optimization seeds. From a 85.4% baseline, final reasoning accuracy averaged 97.5% with the current source and 92.6% with the frozen source. The paired difference is +4.9 percentage points, 95% bootstrap interval [+1.2, +9.7].

The current-source advantage repeated in all three seeds, with a smaller effect than in the exploratory pilot. This supports repeated elicitation through self-generated reasoning in this setting. It does not show that unfiltered self-imitation helps, that short-answer reasoning has been compressed, or that the learning curves have different scaling exponents.

These studies separate elicitation, consolidation, and policy refresh. A successful high-compute answer is not itself a learning result. A better learned answer is not automatically an on-policy advantage. No scaling exponents are fitted here.

Existing information, more useful computation

Each arithmetic program supplies a starting integer and 4, 6, or 8 addition, subtraction, or multiplication operations. All rules are already in the question. The model receives no oracle corrections. Exact answers are used only by an offline evaluator. Plurality selection uses completed answers, includes mistakes, and breaks ties by first occurrence.

The confirmation uses 144 fresh questions, 48 at each depth. The consensus gain over the short response is 87.5 points, 95% paired interval [81.9, 92.4]. All short and sampled reasoning responses completed. Short answers permit 96 new tokens; reasoning permits 512 per attempt. This is an intentionally different inference-compute budget, not a comparison at equal inference cost.

Calibration failures and answer-extraction amendments

The initially screened math-specialized model ignored the short-answer instruction and exhausted the 96-token budget on every calibration response. Its apparent gap was an interface failure, and those runs are retained separately. The general model obeyed short mode. Inspection then found valid explicit final integers without LaTeX boxes; a parser extension was frozen before this fresh confirmation. Original raw responses and strict-box scores remain intact. The alternate permutation-machine task did not qualify. Neither a useful-looking curve nor an exponent was a selection criterion.

Answer-only training suppressed reasoning

Each arm starts from the same pinned Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct weights and sees the same 96 new practice questions, in four shuffled passes. Three seeds vary the ordering and sampling. A separate 144-question test set was frozen before training.

  • Frozen reasoning source: four fresh reasoning samples from the initial model for each scheduled presentation; train the short-answer policy on their plurality answer.
  • Current reasoning source: the same procedure, with the source weights refreshed after each 16-question batch.
  • Direct self-imitation: sample a short response and train on its actual tokens, without correctness selection.

All arms update full model weights with AdamW, learning rate 1e-5, four updates per 16-question batch, FP32 weights/state and BF16 autocast. Completion-token NLL is divided by a fixed normalization; the ordinary LM output head is unchanged. The main pair has matched question, rollout-count, and optimizer schedules. Response lengths and actual compute still differ and are retained in the data.

Final conditionTest: shortTest: reasoningPractice: true answerPractice: latest self-target
Frozen reasoning source0.7%0.5%59.7%64.9%
Current reasoning source0.2%0.2%0.3%72.9%
Direct self-imitation0.0%0.0%0.0%69.3%

Training accuracy and agreement with self-targets distinguish fitting the internal targets from learning an accurate procedure for new questions. Ground-truth diagnostics were computed after the frozen runs and did not influence their targets or hyperparameters.

The common reasoning baseline was 84.0%. After just the first four updates, reasoning-prompt responses shrank from roughly 144 tokens to about 7–9 tokens and accuracy collapsed. The frozen-source learner partly memorized practice answers, but this did not transfer to new programs. The current-source learner also lost the ability to produce useful practice targets. The final short-answer current-minus-frozen difference was -0.5 percentage points, paired 95% interval [-2.3, +0.5]; the main finding is the failure of all three recipes.

Practice retained in context

The initial model also receives 4 or 16 of its own practice examples in context, as either selected final answers or their actual sampled reasoning traces. This is one demonstration sequence and an exploratory transfer check. It is not an independent three-seed replication of the weight-learning result.

ExamplesContextShort accuracyReasoning accuracyShort completion
4answers0.7%0.0%100.0%
4traces0.0%94.4%0.0%
16answers1.4%1.4%100.0%
16traces0.0%94.4%4.2%

With full traces in context, reasoning responses average about 179 tokens with four examples and 152 with sixteen, compared with 144 without examples. Input contexts are also longer. Under the 96-token short-answer limit, completion falls to 0% and 4.2%, respectively. Those short-mode failures are truncations, so they do not show that the model forgot arithmetic. The reasoning improvement is not established at equal total inference compute.

Follow-up: teach the actual reasoning trace

This recipe uses 96 new practice questions, four passes, and a separate 144-question evaluation cohort. The model now trains under its original reasoning prompt on the actual sampled reasoning tokens. The two main arms still select from four samples by internal plurality. The control imitates one unfiltered current-model reasoning trace, including incomplete attempts.

All model weights are updated with AdamW at learning rate 1e-6, one update per batch of 16, and completion NLL divided by the fixed value 128 × batch size. FP32 weights/state, BF16 autocast, and clipping at 1 are retained. The prompt, target representation, update count, learning rate, and normalization all change from the failed recipe. This is a new recipe, not a causal isolation of trace preservation alone.

The current-minus-frozen reasoning difference is +12.5 percentage points, with a paired question-bootstrap 95% interval [+7.6, +18.1]. These intervals describe this test cohort conditional on one realized training run. They do not include training-seed variability.

The raw self-imitation control uses one rollout rather than four. The expected raw score gradient is zero at the sampling parameters under exact matched sampling and likelihood, but finite sampling, numerical precision, clipping, and AdamW can still move the weights. A realized gain or loss in this control is not evidence against that identity.

Confirmation with new questions and three training seeds

The learner, prompts, target rule, 96-question practice budget, four passes, optimizer, response limits, and checkpoints remain unchanged. New cohorts use practice seed 71100 and evaluation seed 71200; optimization seeds 71000–71002 vary ordering and sampling. The one-rollout control is not repeated. All six runs finished before correctness analysis.

Final conditionMean reasoning accuracyThree seed accuraciesMean short accuracyReasoning tokens
Frozen reasoning source92.6%95.8%, 90.3%, 91.7%0.5%150.7
Current reasoning source97.5%97.2%, 97.2%, 97.9%1.6%150.0

This is a fresh-data confirmation for the same architecture. The three seeds share 144 evaluation questions; they are not 432 independent questions. The paired bootstrap resamples seeds and questions, with questions stratified by program length. It is limited by three seeds and one new cohort. Perfect observed scores can produce degenerate bootstrap bands, which do not establish perfect population accuracy.

At the same final presentation budget, the current-source arm used about 9.2% more generation-plus-training input tokens. At the prespecified 192-presentation checkpoint it already achieved 96.5% reasoning accuracy using about 246,000 such tokens; the frozen-source arm reached 92.6% after 384 presentations and about 452,000 tokens. This is favorable under the recorded token-work proxy, but it does not establish a hardware-FLOP scaling law.

An explicit linear mechanism and its limits

The toy assumes a useful internal generator already exists: z is standard Gaussian and x=Az+noise. A separate linear recognition map Bx estimates z. Internally generated (x,z) pairs can train B toward the posterior-mean inverse B*=Aᵀ(AAᵀ+σ²I)⁻¹. The generator has supplied no new observations of the world; it has made existing knowledge available as a supervised target.

E||Bx-z||² = irreducible error + tr((B-B*) C (B-B*)ᵀ)
grad_B(half MSE) = B C - Aᵀ,    C = A Aᵀ + σ²I

Across 32 SGD runs, prediction error falls from 8 to 1.8566, near the optimal 1.8422. Normalized weight overlap reaches 0.9997. Self-imitation supplies no expected corrective gradient; an incorrect generator can actively worsen the inverse.

The toy keeps A fixed. It therefore demonstrates closure of an inference gap but cannot, by itself, explain an advantage from refreshing an autoregressive policy. It also uses a different task from the LLM arithmetic pilot. A complete three-setting equivalence remains a research objective, not an established conclusion.

A linear extension that does test sampler refresh

Keep the same generative model, but initialize a latent particle at the current recognition mean Bx plus Gaussian noise. Take one posterior-refinement step using the model's reconstruction residual and prior, then train B on that sampled particle. The frozen control always initializes at the original B₀x. Both take one posterior step per internal training pair and receive the same questions and coupled randomness; the latent used to generate each input is discarded before target creation.

H = I + AᵀA / σ²,     R = I - δH
z₀ = Bx + ε₀
z₁ = Rz₀ + δAᵀx/σ² + ε₁
Cov(ε₁) = 2δI - δ²H

This transition preserves the exact Gaussian posterior, but one step from an imperfect initialization remains biased. With current initialization, the expected weight error evolves as Eₜ₊₁ = Eₜ − ηδH Eₜ C and approaches zero at stable step sizes. Frozen initialization approaches B = δAᵀ/σ², the mean of its permanently shallow teacher. The prediction is analytic and was recorded before simulation.

At 262,144 internal pairs, current initialization gives mean error 2.1024 versus 5.3060 for frozen initialization, from an initial error of 8. The optimal error is 1.8422. This demonstrates a refresh mechanism without adding facts: better recognition initializes better posterior samples, which further improve recognition.

The posterior-refinement operation is supplied by the assumed useful generative model. It is the extra computation that makes these targets differ from unfiltered recognition samples. This toy models refreshing posterior initialization; it is not a matched autoregressive LLM experiment. Its geometric dynamics and biased frozen limit do not establish different scaling exponents.

What the three settings currently establish

SettingWhat self-generation contributesRemaining limitation
Linear Gaussian learnerInternal latent targets align recognition weights with the implied posterior. A separate posterior-rollout extension benefits from refreshing its initialization.The useful generative model and posterior-refinement operation are supplied; the arithmetic LLM has not been reduced to this mechanism.
LLM in-context learningKeeping full self-generated worked examples improves subsequent reasoning on new arithmetic programs.One exploratory sequence, longer context, no demonstrated short-answer compression.
LLM weight learningFresh versus frozen-source practice is directly compared; the full-trace recipe receives a fresh-data, three-seed confirmation.One architecture, one confirmation cohort, and a short saturating budget range. Short-answer compression still fails.

The shared hypothesis is that computation can expose competence already implicit in a model, then practice can make it easier to use. Shannon information need not increase. A distinct advantage from refreshing the sampler requires additional evidence: useful changes in the model's own practice distribution that improve subsequent learning beyond the frozen-source control.

Reproducibility and resources

Audited 18 learning cases and 90 checkpoints, including every target's source, causal presentation order, counters, matching initial teacher draws, and paired baseline predictions. Final answer-only seed 68000 models, all full-trace pilot models, and confirmation seed 71000 models were copied to shared storage and SHA-256 verified before their jobs exited.

Across screening, confirmation, evaluation, training, and archival, completed allocations totaled 103.5 H100 GPU-minutes. This includes reserved time for evaluation and model copies, rather than only optimizer work. New paid API/Vast spending was $0.
